planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; transplant once nights stay reliably above 55-60F. Thai Dragon is a hybrid cayenne-type chile bred for a more upright, compact habit than traditional Thai bird peppers, making it easier to manage in beds and containers.

directions: Transplant into warm, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, spacing plants to allow good air circulation in humid climates. Thai Dragon produces narrow, 2-3 inch fruit held upright above the foliage in heavy clusters, ripening from green to glossy red with intense, lingering heat well above standard cayenne types. The compact, well-branched plants are productive over a long season and tolerate container culture better than many Southeast Asian chile types. Harvest fruit at any stage for fresh use, or let clusters ripen fully red and string them for drying and grinding into chile flakes.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Thai Dragon Hot Pepper
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm soil after frost danger has passed. Wenk's Yellow Hot is an Iowa heirloom maintained and distributed through Seed Savers Exchange, prized for dependable production of tapering yellow hot peppers.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, spacing plants to accommodate the tall, productive habit. Wenk's Yellow Hot bears tapering, 3-4 inch fruit that ripens from pale yellow-green to a bright golden yellow, with a brisk, moderate-to-hot heat well suited to pickling and hot sauce. The vigorous, upright plants set fruit heavily over a long season and hold up well in home garden conditions without special care. This Midwestern family heirloom has been passed down and preserved through seed-saving networks rather than commercial breeding.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Wenk's Yellow Hot Pepper

common_name: Hinkelhatz Pepper (Pennsylvania Dutch Chicken Heart Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil has warmed. Hinkelhatz is a Pennsylvania Dutch heirloom whose name translates roughly to 'chicken heart,' describing the small, pointed, heart-like shape of its fruit.

directions: Transplant into well-drained garden soil in full sun once nights stay warm, giving plants room to branch and set their heavy fruit load. Hinkelhatz produces abundant small, tapered, heart-shaped peppers about one to two inches long that ripen from yellow to orange to red, carrying noticeable heat in a tiny package. Long grown in Pennsylvania German communities, the fruits are traditionally strung and dried or steeped into hot pepper vinegar used to season greens and preserved foods. The bushy, productive plants continue setting new fruit clusters through the growing season with minimal maintenance.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all danger of frost has passed. Chile Japones is a slender cayenne-relative widely used dried in both Mexican and East Asian cooking despite its name referencing Japan.

directions: Transplant into warm, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants to support their tall, productive growth. Chile Japones yields narrow, two to three inch fruit in heavy clusters that ripen from green to deep red and carry sharp, cayenne-level heat with a clean, slightly smoky flavor once dried. The small fruit dries quickly and easily on the plant or after harvest, making it a reliable choice for home-dried chile flakes, infused oils, and the fried dried chiles used in stir-fries and salsas. Vigorous, upright plants tolerate heat well and continue producing new flushes of fruit through a long summer season.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm soil after frost danger has passed. Hot Portugal is a New England heirloom long maintained in Portuguese-American gardening communities of southern New England.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the soil has warmed, giving plants ample room for their tall, branching growth. Hot Portugal produces long, tapering fruit six to eight inches in length that ripens from green to red with substantial, lingering heat similar to a large cayenne. Fruits are traditionally steeped whole in vinegar to make the hot pepper vinegar splashed over fish, greens, and beans in New England Portuguese-American kitchens, though they are equally good fresh, roasted, or dried. The vigorous plants bear heavily over a long season and handle humid summer conditions well.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Hot Portugal Pepper

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger has passed. Super Chili is an All-America Selections award-winning hybrid bred for a compact habit and heavy, early fruit set, making it a long-standing favorite for containers.

directions: Transplant into well-drained soil in full sun or grow in a large container, spacing plants to let the compact, bushy habit fill in. Super Chili sets large numbers of small, slender, upward-facing fruit that ripen quickly from green to bright red, carrying sharp, well above cayenne-level heat in a two to three inch pod. The dense fruit set against dark green foliage also makes this an attractive dual-purpose ornamental and culinary pepper for patios and small beds. Harvest continuously through the season to encourage further flowering and fruit set, or let a flush ripen fully red for drying.
sources: Burpee Seeds — Super Chili Hybrid Pepper

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; transplant after frost danger passes or grow in a decorative container. Calico is grown chiefly for its variegated cream, green, and purple foliage rather than for culinary fruit production.

directions: Transplant into well-drained potting mix or garden soil in full sun, where bright light keeps the foliage variegation most vivid. Calico's cream, green, and purple-splashed leaves provide season-long color even before fruiting begins, and the small, conical fruits continue the theme as they ripen through purple, cream, orange, and red in the same cluster. The dense, mounding habit suits mixed containers, hanging baskets, and bedding borders as much as any flowering annual. Fruit is pungently hot and edible but is typically treated as a colorful accent rather than a kitchen crop; pinch growing tips early to encourage fuller branching.
sources: university extension bedding plant trial notes
